opening.headline: Learn why an AI may appear to lose earlier instructions in a long document by exploring the units it reads and the amount of text it can process at once.
body: You may have pasted a long document into a generative AI chat, placed instructions at the beginning, and received an answer that did not follow them. Often, the issue is not deliberate disregard for your instructions but limits on how the model reads text and how much it can handle at once.

This lesson explores how models process input and output in units called tokens rather than individual characters, and how both share a limit called the context window. We then compare providing a full 100-page report with providing a summary, so you can decide which approach fits a task.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Understand the relationship between input length and response quality

screens.title: When a long document pushes instructions out of view
screens.lead: First, let's look at a situation that many people face. Read the scene below and think about what the problem is.

visual.alt: A scene with a long document, a request speech bubble pasted with instructions at the beginning, and a short answer speech bubble that differs from the instructions placed above and below.
labels: Summarize in three lines and organize them in a table.
Answer translated directly from the middle of the document

paragraphs: An employee pasted the entire report into the AI chat window. At the beginning, I wrote, “Summary in three lines and organize them in a table.” However, the answer that came back was not a table, but line text that almost exactly translated the content in the middle of the document.

When something like this happens, it's easy to feel like "the AI forgot my instructions." But models don't remember or forget like people do. There is a limit to the amount the model can accept at one time, and that amount is calculated in units other than characters.

There are two questions to be answered in this lesson. First, in what units does the model read the text? Second, how much can be seen at one time, and how is that limit divided between input and output?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Which would have a greater impact on the results: the fact that the instructions were at the very beginning of the document or the fact that the document was very long? You will be able to answer this question again at the end of class.

screens.outro: Let me start by recalling your own experience.

screens.title: Reflect on your experience
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: When you paste a long text into an AI, have you ever found the answer to be interrupted or strange?
items.answer: This experience is common. A choppy answer is usually a sign that the model did not have enough space to write an answer, and an odd answer can be a sign that needed information was outside of what the model could see. The starting point of this class is to determine which one is which.

items.prompt: What was the problem at that time was when the pasted text was long, or when the conversation continued for a long time?
items.answer: Both have the same cause. Even if one article is long or multiple short articles are piled up, the total amount of text that the model sees at once increases. So a single long input and a long conversation are accounted for by the same limit problem.

items.prompt: Did you think that the number of characters and the amount of AI processing were the same thing?
items.answer: Many people guess based on the number of characters or pages. However, the model calculates in units called tokens. Even in texts of the same length, the number of tokens may vary depending on the language and content, so we will look at this unit in the following screen.

screens.outro: Now that we've organized the experience, let's start by checking the units in which the model reads the text.

screens.title: The model reads tokens, not letters
screens.lead: Hover over or select an underlined term in the description below to see a short description. Check the terms one by one.

visual.alt: Illustration showing how one line of English example sentences is divided into token chips.
labels: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.
One token is approximately 4 letters, and 100 tokens are approximately 60 to 80 English words.

data.text: Generative AI models process inputs and outputs in units called token. A token may be a single character like "z," or a word like "cat." Longer words are split into multiple token units. The process of dividing a sentence into token units is called tokenization, and the complete set of token units used by the model is referred to as vocabulary. The Gemini document states that one token is roughly equivalent to four characters, and that 100 token units correspond to approximately 60–80 English words. This value is only an estimate based on estimate, so the exact quantity should be verified by direct counting. Additionally, the number of token units becomes part of the basis for calculating call costs.

terms.tip: It is the basic unit through which a model processes input and output. A single letter, a word, or part of a word can all be tokens.
This is the process of dividing a sentence into token units that are processed by the model. The standard is different from how people read words with spacing.
In English, it is vocabulary. Points to the set of all tokens used by the model.
This is an approximate conversion, not an exact value. For important requests, check by manually counting the number of tokens.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the units, let's see how the same content is counted differently depending on the language and input type.

screens.title: Count tokens for an accurate estimate
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how to check the number of tokens and the differences in what is calculated.

tabs.label: Differences depending on language
tabs.body: The approximate value "one token is approximately 4 characters" is an explanation based on the English language. Even sentences with the same meaning are split into tokens differently depending on the language, so even if the number of characters is the same, the number of tokens can vary. When dealing with long texts in languages ​​other than English, such as Korean, it is safer to actually count rather than estimate.

tabs.label: Count in advance
tabs.body: Gemini API provides `count_tokens`. When you call with input to be included in the request, it returns the total number of tokens for that input only. The documentation explains that it is used to check the size of the input by calling it before actually sending the request. If you count a long document before loading it, you'll know in advance if you'll hit the limit.

tabs.label: Check your usage
tabs.body: After sending the request, you can see the `usage` information in the response. It contains input tokens (`total_input_tokens`), output tokens (`total_output_tokens`), thought tokens (`total_thought_tokens`), cached content tokens (`total_cached_tokens`), tool usage tokens (`total_tool_use_tokens`), and full tokens (`total_tokens`). It's like a statement showing where the token was spent in one call.

tabs.label: Input outside text
tabs.body: All inputs and outputs from the Gemini API are processed as tokens. This applies not only to text, but also to non-text input such as image files. So, if a document contains many pictures or pictures, it is difficult to guess the overall size just by looking at the number of characters.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the context window, the limit that tokens create together.

screens.title: Input and output share the context window
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the importance of input. You can see how the space left in the output changes as the input grows.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the context window as one long horizontal bar, split between input and output.
labels: Context window (total amount of tokens visible at one time)
Output (including answers, tokens used for thinking inside the model)

data.controlLabel: Share of the context window used by input

stops.body: If the input only takes up a small portion of the window, there is plenty of room for the output. This may be the case if you only include a short question and a few paragraphs of required information. The model can write long enough answers, and there is no shortage of tokens for the model to use to think internally before answering.

This is when the input takes up around half of the window. From this point on, the output margin is noticeably reduced. Since input and output share the same window, remember that the amount available for output decreases as much as you spend on input.

If the input fills most of the window, less space is left for the output. The answer may be interrupted or may not contain enough information. Even as the conversation gets longer, previous information continues to pile up, creating the same situation.

The official model table lists a context window of around 1M tokens and a maximum output of 128K tokens. OpenAI's model table has a model with a context window of 1.05M. No matter how big your window is, it's not infinite, so it's up to you to decide what and how much to put in it.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the concept of limits, let's apply them to real cases.

screens.title: Commentary: When inserting the entire 100-page report
screens.lead: The instructor explains the initial situation step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Estimating Request A by Tokens
steps.body: Request A is the entire 100-page report and one line of instructions at the beginning. Since the number of pages is not a unit used by the model, it must be converted to a token. 100 pages can contain tens of thousands of English words, which can be tens to hundreds of thousands of tokens. The exact value can be found by counting in the same way as `count_tokens`.

steps.title: Input reduces output space
steps.body: If the input takes up a significant portion of the window, less space is left for the output. Answers that create and summarize tables need some length, but if space is limited, the answer may be short or disconnected.

steps.title: As the conversation continues, the front part gets pushed aside.
steps.body: If you paste the report and continue asking questions multiple times, the previous information will continue to accumulate. If the limit is exceeded, the model may become invisible because it is pushed to the very front. The instructions written at the very beginning of the document are at the very beginning.

steps.title: So the instructions seem weak.
steps.body: Ultimately, “answers that seem to have forgotten the instructions” may not be due to a problem with the model’s memory, but rather because the instructions have been pushed out of the model’s field of view or buried in the volume of documentation. A model cannot react to something it cannot see.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: It is safer to place instructions close to the question and include only the parts that are absolutely necessary. First consider whether you need to put the whole thing in, and if so, count the length to see how close you are to the limit.

screens.outro: Next, let's compare it to a request that achieves the same goal with a summary.

screens.title: Commentary: Comparison to requesting a summary
screens.lead: Switch between the two requests and compare their input size, advantages, and limitations. It's good to note that input and response quality are simply not proportional. The instructor's conclusions are summarized at the end.

states.label: Request A: Full Document
states.body: Put in the entire 100-page report and ask questions. The advantage is that every detail is in view of the model. The limitation is that there are so many input tokens that the output margin is reduced, and as the limit is approached, the front end may be pushed out or instructions may be buried. This approach may be necessary for questions that require evidence scattered throughout the report. In this case as well, it is safer to repeat the instructions closer to the question rather than leaving them at the front of the document.

states.label: Request B: Summary
states.body: Send questions like a summary containing only key paragraphs. The advantage is that fewer input tokens free up the window and free up output space. The limitation is that the model cannot see details that are missing from the summary. For questions that ask for the overall flow or key conclusions, this approach is often sufficient. However, since the summary is the result of someone's already selected choices, you must first check whether the choices fit the question.

screens.outro: I will conclude by organizing the comparisons into one standard.

screens.title: Criteria for looking at input length and response quality together
screens.lead: I will summarize what I have seen so far into one judgment standard.

paragraphs: Just because the input is longer does not mean that the answer will be worse, or conversely, the longer the input, the more accurate it will be. What is important is whether the necessary information is within limits and whether the information is visible to the model.

That's why it's helpful to get into the habit of checking three things before sending a request: Is the entire document necessary for this question, or is just part of it sufficient? Are the instructions close to the question? Is the input length close to the limit?

After answering these three questions, the report case we looked at earlier will seem to change from a question of “the AI forgot” to a question of “how to structure the input.” The conclusion of this class is to distinguish between questions that are necessary in their entirety and questions that are sufficient in part, and check the length by directly counting it like `count_tokens`.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The model reads tokens rather than characters, and there is a limit to how much can be viewed at one time. Input and output share their limits.

glossary.def: It is the basic unit through which a model processes input and output. It can be a single letter, a word, or part of a word.
This is the process of dividing a sentence into token units that are processed by the model.
This is the limit on the total amount of tokens the model can see at one time. Input and output are used together.
This is a feature that counts the number of tokens in the input before sending a request in the Gemini API.

misconceptions.fact: A token can be a single letter, a word, or part of a longer word. The splitting method varies depending on the language, so the number of tokens cannot be determined based on the number of words.

misconceptions.myth: The context window only applies to input.
misconceptions.fact: Input and output share the same window. The larger the input, the less space is available for your answer.

misconceptions.myth: If the window is large, the quality is the same no matter how long it is.
misconceptions.fact: Even if it's within the limits, results can vary depending on what you put in and where the instructions are. It is safer to insert only as much as needed and check by counting the length.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The model reads and writes token by token, not by character.
The context window is limited to the amount that can be viewed at one time, and both input and output are used together.
Longer conversations can push the first part out of bounds and make your instructions seem weak.
Enter only as many tokens as you need, and check the number of tokens by counting them rather than guessing.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which inputs I use in my work might be subject to limits?

title: Tokens and context windows: how models read

checks.q: What is the most appropriate change in the model's answer as the input text becomes very long?
options: Since input and output share the same window, space for answers is reduced.
The longer the input, the more context the model gets so the answer is always accurate.
The output limit is independent of the input, so the input length has no effect on the answer.
Longer inputs result in fewer tokens, lowering processing costs.
checks.explain: The context window is the total amount of tokens the model can see at one time, and is used together with inputs and outputs. So, the larger the input, the smaller the output margin.

wrong.1: Longer doesn't always mean more accurate. It is important that the necessary information is within limits.
wrong.2: Input and output share the same window.
wrong.3: If the input is long, the number of tokens increases.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match the following concepts and explanations
right: Ability to pre-count the number of input tokens before sending the request
The process of breaking sentences into units that the model can process
Total amount of tokens the model can see at one time
The basic unit by which a model processes input and output
checks.explain: A token is a unit of processing, a context window is the total amount that can be viewed at a time, and tokenization is a truncation process. For inputs where the number of tokens can vary, such as Korean, it is safe to count them with count_tokens.
checks.intro: Organize terms by pairing concepts with explanations. Results are not recorded.
